Directions (115-120): Study the following information carefully and answer the questions
that follow.
A comprehensive study was conducted across five major tech hubs—Hyderabad, Pune,
Ahmedabad, Gurgaon, and Noida—to analyse the shift in preference from traditional Internal
Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles to Electric Vehicles (EVs). In Hyderabad, 20,000 people
participated in the study, and it was found that 45% of them preferred transitioning to an EV.
In Pune, where 18,000 people were surveyed, a total of 10,800 individuals expressed their
preference for EVs. Moving to Ahmedabad, 15,000 people were surveyed, out of which 6,000
respondents stated they did not prefer EVs, opting for traditional vehicles instead. In Gurgaon,
the survey covered 12,000 people, but the results showed a strong leaning toward tradition, as
80% of the participants preferred ICE vehicles over electric ones. Finally, in Noida, 16,000
people were surveyed, and the percentage of people who preferred EVs was calculated to be
exactly equal to the average of the EV preference percentages recorded in Hyderabad and Pune.

XXVI. In 2025, five National Law Universities—NLSIU Bangalore, NLU Delhi, NALSAR Hyderabad,
NLU Jodhpur and NLU Bhopal—formed the National Law Research Consortium (NALRC) to
develop artificial intelligence tools for legal research, judicial analytics and policy drafting.
The project continued for three years. Since universities joined the consortium at different
points of time, the final commercialization revenue generated by the project was distributed
according to each university's effective contribution ratio, defined as: Number of Researchers x
Duration of Participation. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The consortium report stated that NLSIU Bangalore deployed 334% more researchers than
NLU Delhi. NALSAR Hyderabad deployed 25% more researchers than NLSIU Bangalore.
NLU Jodhpur deployed 20% fewer researchers than NALSAR Hyderabad. The number of
researchers deployed by NLU Jodhpur and NLU Bhopal was in the ratio 1/4: 1/5. The total
number of researchers from all the law universities combined is 96. NLSIU Bangalore and
NLU Delhi participated throughout the three-year duration of the project. NALSAR
Hyderabad joined after the completion of the first year. NLU Jodhpur joined six months after

second year. At the conclusion of the project, the consortium generated %4.02 crore through
licensing agreements and commercialization of research outputs. The revenue was distributed
among participating universities according to their effective contribution ratio.

XIX. In a large research institute worked a team of analysts who preferred using symbols instead of
long descriptions to denote professional relationships. Over time, these symbols became a shared
code within the institute. For example, when they wrote A @ B, it meant that A was the supervisor
of B, while A # B indicated that A was the mentor of B. The symbol A % B was used to show that A
was the junior associate of B, and collaboration between colleagues was represented by A & B,

organisational structure using only these symbols. “See this,” said one analyst, writing R@S & T

passages.QUA-P0057: Following a national directive issued by the Prime Minister to reduce fossil fuel consumption, six ministries - Transport, Defence, Agriculture, Health, Infrastructure, and Education - implemented measures to cut down on the usage of petrol and diesel. The total petrol and diesel consumption per month of all the ministries together before the directive was 550,000 liters and 900,000 liters, respectively. The Education ministry consumed 50000 liters of petrol and the Defence ministry consumed twice that quantity whereas the ratio of petrol consumption by the Transport, Agriculture, Health, and Infrastructure ministries was 6 : 4 : 3 : 7, respectively. The Transport and Infrastructure ministries consumed 200,000 liters of diesel each whereas the ratio of diesel consumption by the Defence, Agriculture, Health, and Education ministries was 9 : 7 : 5 : 4, respectively. After taking corrective measures, there was a total reduction of 20% in the petrol consumption by all ministries. Now, the Education and Defence ministries respectively consumed 45000 liters and 85000 liters of petrol whereas the ratio of petrol consumption of the Transport, Agriculture, Health, and Infrastructure ministries became 9 : 6 : 5 : 11, respectively. Similarly there was a total reduction of 16⅔% in the diesel consumption after corrective measures were put in place. Now the Health, and Education ministries consumed 80000 and 70000 liters of diesel, respectively whereas the ratio of the diesel consumption by the Transport, Defence, Agriculture, and Infrastructure ministries became 16 : 15 : 11 : 18, respectively. The cost per litre of petrol is Rs.100 and that of diesel is Rs.90. A ministry is considered “efficient” if it reduces at least 20% of its total fuel consumption. Also, Savings = reduction in consumption × respective fuel cost

passages.QUA-P0066:
Direction (111-116): Study the following information carefully and answer the
      questions given below.
      Digital literacy plays a critical role in socio-economic development, enabling access to
      education, financial services, and governance. In India, however, a significant disparity
      exists in the extent and nature of internet access and digital skills between urban and
      rural populations. While urban populations generally have better access to high-speed
      broadband, subsidized connectivity schemes, and higher levels of digital competence,
      rural populations face challenges such as limited network infrastructure, high device
      costs, and lower awareness about digital services. This urban-rural divide in digital
      adoption highlights the broader issue of digital inequality, making it essential to analyse
      the factors contributing to this gap and explore strategies for more inclusive digital
      protection. A nationwide digital access survey was conducted.
      The survey covered 1,20,000 adults across urban and rural areas. Urban residents
      formed 60% of the sample (that is, 72,000 people) while rural residents made up 40%
      (that is, 48,000 people). In each area, digital status was classified under four heads –
      Daily Internet Users, Infrequent Users, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet), and
      Digitally Excluded.
      In urban areas, Daily Internet Users accounted for 45% of the urban population,
      Infrequent Users for 25%, Basic Smartphone Users (no internet) for 10%, and the
      remaining 20% were Digitally Excluded. In rural areas, where digital access is generally
      lower, Daily Internet Users stood at 15%, Infrequent Users at 15%, Basic Smartphone
      Users (no internet) at 25%, while 45% were Digitally Excluded. For this survey,
      "Digitally Enabled" includes everyone who uses the internet (Daily + Infrequent users),
      and "Digitally Excluded" indicates those with no regular digital engagement (Basic
      Smartphone + Excluded).
passages.QUA-P0067:
I.	VeloTech Assemblies, a mid-sized cycle manufacturing unit located in an industrial belt near
Pune, keeps meticulous weekly production records to monitor its output efficiency. The factory
operates under an internal benchmark of 1,200 cycles per week, which was set by the
management as the minimum threshold for profitable operation. Each cycle manufactured at
the unit is priced at 71,500 at the factory gate.
According to the production log maintained over five consecutive weeks, the factory produced
700 cycles in the 1st week, a figure that fell significantly below the internal benchmark.
Performance improved sharply in the 2nd week, with output rising to 1,400 cycles, more than
doubling the previous week's production. However, the 3rd week witnessed a dip, with only
1,000 cycles produced, followed by a further decline to 900 cycles in the 4th week. The factory
staged a recovery in the 5th week, recording its best performance of the period with 1,600
cycles — the highest weekly output and the only week to exceed the y-axis maximum of 1,600
on the production chart.
The management observed that production remained inconsistent across the period, with the
first and fourth weeks falling considerably below the benchmark while only the second and
fifth weeks managed to surpass it. The finance team was tasked with preparing a revenue
analysis based on these five weeks of production data to present before the board at the next
quarterly review.

bullets of three types i.e., Lead Round Nose (LRN), Semi-Jacketed (SJ) and FMJ (Full Metal
Jacket) fired by them during the respective wars. The following information provides the
percentage by which the number of LRN bullets fired is less than the number of SJ bullets
fired, and the percentage by which the number of FMJ bullets fired is more than the number
of LRN bullets fired, during the respective wars.
The first dataset indicates the percentage by which the number of LRN bullets fired was
less than the number of SJ bullets fired. These percentages were 52% in 1947, 16% in
1965, and 36% in 1971.
The second dataset shows the percentage by which the number of FMJ bullets fired was
more than the number of LRN bullets fired. These values were 140% in 1947, 60% in 1965,
and 80% in 1971.

during 1947, which was 9990 fewer than that during 1965.

XXI. In the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak, the demand for sanitizers surged sharply across the country.
Three newly established companies — A, B, and C — began manufacturing sanitizer using two main
ingredients: Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) and gel base.
Company A produced 240 litres of sanitizer in which the ratio of IPA to gel base was 9 : 11. Later, the
manufacturer added an additional quantity of pure IPA to this mixture. As a result, the proportion of
gel base in the final mixture decreased to exactly one-third of the total.
Company B had two separate vessels — P and Q. Vessel P contained 70 litres of pure IPA, while vessel
Q contained 40 litres of pure gel base. First, 24 litres of IPA from vessel P was transferred to vessel Q.
Then, 18 litres of the resulting mixture in vessel Q was transferred back to vessel P.
Company C began with 810 litres of sanitizer containing IPA and gel base in the ratio 4 : 5. The
manufacturer replaced the mixture with pure gel base in three successive operations: first, 180 litres of
the mixture was removed and replaced with gel base; then, 324 litres was removed and replaced in the
same way; finally, 135 litres was removed and replaced with gel base.

XX. Before the festive shopping weekend in Udaipur, Riya, Dev, Imran, and Kavya were helping
set up a handcrafted lifestyle fair near the lakeside promenade. Each display section had a
different two-dimensional shape, and the organisers carefully noted the measurements to
estimate area, perimeter, flooring, and decoration costs.
Riya was in charge of a rectangular carpet zone for handwoven rugs. Its length was 24 m and
breadth was 15 m. Dev arranged a circular sitting area for visitors around a tea counter, and
its radius was 7 m. Imran designed a triangular showcase section for wooden decor items, with
side lengths 13 m, 14 m, and 15 m. Kavya marked out a semicircular floral entrance patch
whose diameter was 14 m.
To improve movement around the fair, the organisers planned a 2 m wide walking strip all
around the outside of the rectangular carpet zone. They also decided to place a square platform
of side 8 m inside the circular sitting area for live craft demonstrations, while the remaining
portion of the circle would be covered with grass mats.
Later, the event manager observed that the rectangular carpet zone could be fully covered
using square mats of side 3 m without any cutting or overlap. She also noted that the
triangular showcase area and the rectangular zone could be compared to understand how
much more space one offered than the other. In addition, the full boundary of the semicircular
entrance patch had to be lined with decorative lamps, making it useful for calculating the total
length of border decoration required.

XX. Techno Manufacturing Pvt. Ltd., a Pune-based industrial equipment manufacturer, conducted
an organisational audit in the first quarter of 2026 to assess human resource deployment
across departments. The company employs 8,000 workers spread across six functional areas—
Production, Accounts, Sales, Marketing, Human Resources (HR), and Information Technology
(IT). The audit aimed to evaluate workforce allocation for optimisation, skill development, and
future recruitment planning.
The Production department accounted for the largest share at 32%, reflecting the company’s
manufacturing-intensive operations. The Accounts department comprised 18% of the
workforce, highlighting the scale and complexity of financial management. Sales employed
16%, while Marketing accounted for 14%, supporting revenue generation and brand
development. The HR department made up 12% of employees, managing recruitment, training,
and compliance. The IT department, responsible for digital infrastructure and cybersecurity,
represented the smallest share at 8%.
Overall, the audit found the workforce distribution to be broadly aligned with operational
needs, though it recommended a gradual expansion of IT staffing to support ongoing digital
transformation.

tonnes) through different modes—Road, Rail, Inland Waterways, Air Cargo, and Pipelines. The

freight distribution.

Road transports 2,400 thousand tonnes, Rail 1,600 thousand tonnes, Inland Waterways 700
thousand tonnes, Air Cargo 200 thousand tonnes, and Pipelines 600 thousand tonnes, making the
quarterly total 5,500 thousand tonnes.

thousand tonnes, Inland Waterways improve to 800 thousand tonnes, Air Cargo increases to 250
thousand tonnes, and Pipelines to 650 thousand tonnes, bringing the total to 5,800 thousand

passages.QUA-P0101:
XXI. New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has said that the recently finalised Free Trade
Agreement with India will boost exports and open new opportunities for farmers, growers and
businesses, describing the pact as a landmark deal with one of the world’s fastest-growing major
economies. India and New Zealand have concluded negotiations on the FTA, which is expected to take
effect in seven to eight months. The agreement aims to enhance market access and promote
investment flows between the two countries, including a foreign direct investment commitment of $20
billion over a period of 15 years. "We've concluded a Free Trade Agreement with India. This will open
doors for New Zealand farmers, growers, and businesses - boosting exports, creating jobs, and lifting
incomes to help all Kiwis get ahead," New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in a post on
social media on Tuesday. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Luxon held a telephone conversation last
month before announcing the successful conclusion of the trade deal. This is India’s third free trade
agreement in recent months, following a similar pact with the United Kingdom in July and another
with Oman in December. The agreement with Oman will give India more temporary employment visas
and easier access for pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Describing the pact with India as a
"landmark deal" with the world’s fastest-growing big economy, Luxon said it would create opportunities
for jobs, exports and growth for all New Zealanders. He noted that engagement with India had been
"intensive" and said his government has worked extremely hard to prioritise and invest in the
relationship since day one. The result of this engagement is a "high-quality" trade agreement, he said
in a video posted on his social media handle. Describing India as a "trusted partner", Luxon added that
the trade deal will deliver deep and lasting benefits for New Zealand. Negotiations for the trade
agreement were initiated during Luxon’s visit to India in March 2025, when the two leaders agreed on
concluding the FTA. The pact is also expected to help Indian exporters, who are reeling under the
impact of 50 per cent tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on Indian goods, by enabling them
to diversify shipments in the Oceania region.

zealand-free-trade-agreement-set-to-boost-exports-says-pm-luxon/cid/ 2141362
passages.QUA-P0102:
XVIII. Indian politics has found an unlikely mascot in the cockroach — stubborn, reviled, and
considered indestructible. The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, is not a formal political party
but an online satirical movement that emerged after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant
allegedly compared unemployed young people gravitating toward journalism and activism
with cockroaches and parasites during a court hearing. Though he later clarified that his
remarks were directed specifically at those with "fake and bogus degrees," the comment had
already ignited a firestorm online. Within days, the CJP — created by Abhijeet Dipke, a
political communications strategist and student at Boston University — amassed tens of
thousands of sign-ups, inspired the hashtag #MainBhiCockroach, and drew endorsements
from senior opposition politicians including Akhilesh Yadav and Mahua Moitra.
The movement's growth was striking in both speed and scale. The CJP's Instagram account
crossed 10 million followers within a week, surpassing the official account of the BJP — widely
regarded as the world's largest political party by membership — which stood at around 8.7
million. Simultaneously, the CJP's X account, which had accumulated over 200,000 followers,
was withheld from Indian users "in response to a legal demand." The CJP's membership
criteria are deliberately absurdist: being unemployed, lazy, chronically online, and possessing

"the ability to rant professionally." Its website describes itself as "the voice of the lazy and
unemployed" and invites those "tired of pretending everything is fine" to join.
Critics have questioned the movement's spontaneity, pointing to Dipke's prior association with
the Aam Aadmi Party and characterising the CJP as carefully packaged digital politics rather
than genuine grassroots rebellion. Dipke himself, however, insists the idea began as a joke and
grew beyond anything he anticipated. The broader context gives the movement weight beyond
its satirical packaging. India has one of the world's youngest populations, with roughly half its
1.4 billion people under 30 years of age. Yet formal political participation among the young
remains thin: a recent survey found that 29% of young Indians avoided political engagement
entirely, while only 11% belonged to any political party. Across South Asia, youth-led protests
have already unseated governments in Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bangladesh. India has so far
avoided comparable upheaval, but the underlying pressures — unemployment, inequality, and
the sense that education no longer guarantees stability — are identical. As Dipke put it, "Gen
Z has given up on traditional political parties and wants to create its own political front in a
language they understand." [Word Count: 403]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from:
https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz72y11jjq1lo

XVI. A survey was conducted in a semi-urban region to study the distribution of literate individuals across
various age groups. The findings of the survey are summarized using a histogram, which classifies the
population based on age and the corresponding number of literate people.
According to the report, the 10-15 years age group accounts for 350 literate individuals, indicating a
moderate level of literacy among early adolescents. A significant rise is observed in the 15—20 years age
group, which records the highest number of literate people at 900, reflecting increased educational
participation during this stage.
The number of literate individuals shows a gradual decline in higher age groups. The 20-25 years age
group consists of 800 literate people, followed by 650 in the 25-30 years group and 600 in the 30-35
years age bracket. This trend suggests a steady reduction in literacy numbers as age increases beyond
early adulthood.
Further analysis reveals that the 35-40 years age group has 500 literate individuals, while the 40—45
years age group records the lowest count of 300 literate people. This decline may be attributed to
limited access to education in earlier decades.

passages.QUA-P0106: Sunrise General Hospital is a 500-bed multi-specialty private hospital. Its annual performance is reviewed quarter-by-quarter: Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4 across three departments: General Medicine (GM), Orthopaedics (Ortho), and Maternity, and Gynaecology (M&G). The hospital measures performance using the percentage of total beds that are occupied on an average per day during a quarter (Bed Occupancy Rate (BOR)) and average revenue per occupied bed per day (ARPB). Q1: The overall BOR was 60%. General Medicine occupied half of the total occupied beds, Orthopaedics occupied one-third, and the remaining occupied beds belonged to M&G. The ARPB for GM in Q1 was Rs. 8,000/day, Orthopaedics' ARPB was 25% higher than GM's, and M&G's ARPB was Rs. 6,000/day. Q2: The overall BOR improved to 72%. GM's occupied beds grew by 20% over Q1, Orthopaedics' occupied beds remained the same as Q1, and M&G took all remaining occupied beds. The ARPB of every department rose uniformly by 10% over Q1 values. Q3: The overall BOR rose to 80%. The ratio of occupied beds across GM : Ortho : M&G in Q3 was 5 : 2 : 3. GM's ARPB fell by 5% from its Q2 value, Ortho's ARPB stayed flat at its Q2 level, and M&G's ARPB rose by 20% over Q2. Q4: The overall BOR was 70%. GM's occupied beds were 10% fewer than Q3, Ortho's occupied beds rose by 25% over Q3, and M&G's occupied beds made up the remainder to satisfy the BOR. Each department's ARPB in Q4 was the simple average of its Q2 and Q3 ARPB.
passages.QUA-P0107:
XXI. Vanguard Solutions, a diversified corporate entity with a total workforce of 8,000 employees, has
recently released its annual human resources report detailing the distribution of personnel across
its six primary operational departments. The company's organizational structure is divided into
Production, Accounts, Sales, Marketing, HR, and IT, each playing a critical role in its business
ecosystem.
The Production department forms the backbone of the company's operations, employing 32% of the
total workforce. This heavy investment in production staff underscores the company's
manufacturing focus. Following production, the Accounts department holds the second-largest
share with 18% of the workforce, reflecting the administrative complexity of managing such a
large-scale operation.
The sales and marketing functions are split into two distinct departments. The Sales department,
responsible for direct revenue generation, employs 16% of the staff, while the Marketing
department, which focuses on brand strategy and market outreach, comprises 14% of the
workforce.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The HR department, tasked with managing personnel and recruitment, accounts for 12% of the
total workforce. Finally, theIT department, which supports the company's technological
infrastructure, has the smallest workforce share at 8%, indicating a lean technical team relative to
the massive production base.
Together, these six departments—Production (32%), Accounts (18%), Sales (16%), Marketing
(14%), HR (12%), and IT (8%)—account for the entire workforce of 8,000 employees, each
contributing to the company's integrated operational framework.
passages.QUA-P0108: A retail store sells five items — laptops, smartphones, headphones, tablets, and smartwatches. Each item is strategically priced by marking it above the cost price and then offering discounts to attract customers. A profit is earned when the selling price exceeds the cost price, while a loss occurs when heavy discounts reduce the selling price below the cost price. High-demand items, such as smartphones, often provide better profit margins, whereas accessories may be discounted more aggressively. By balancing discounts and profit margins, the store aims to maximize overall profit while remaining competitive. Careful pricing ensures sustainability, customer satisfaction, and steady revenue growth in a competitive market. The laptop has a marked price of Rs. 65,000, and after offering a discount of 20%, the shopkeeper earns a profit of Rs. 2,000. The cost price of the smartwatch is half the cost price of the tablet, and after selling the smartwatch at a discount of 40% on the marked price, the shopkeeper incurs a loss of 10%. The tablet is sold for Rs. 23,800 after a discount of 15% on the marked price, and the shopkeeper earns a profit of 19%. The cost price of the smartphone is equal to the sum of the cost prices of the tablet and the smartwatch. The shopkeeper marks the smartphone at 40% above its cost price, and after offering a discount on the marked price, he earns a profit of 5%. The headphone is marked 50% above the cost price, and by selling it for Rs. 4,200, the shopkeeper earns a profit of 5%.

passages.QUA-P0114:
XX, Prakriti Nagar's Solid Waste Department collected 3,000 tonnes of municipal waste in a day
from four sources: Residential Areas, Markets, Institutions, and Construction Clusters. The
waste collected from these four sources was in the ratio 8:4:3:5 respectively.
Each source had a different level of source segregation. The segregation rate was 60 percent
for Residential Areas, 75 percent for Markets, 50 percent for Institutions, and 20 percent for
Construction Clusters. Segregated waste was divided into wet waste, dry recyclable waste, and
inert waste. In Residential Areas, the segregated waste consisted of 55 percent wet waste, 35
percent dry recyclable waste, and the remainder inert waste. In Markets, the segregated waste
was divided among wet, dry recyclable, and inert waste in the ratio 6:3:1. In Institutions, 30
percent of segregated waste was wet, 50 percent was dry recyclable, and 20 percent was inert.
In Construction Clusters, 10 percent of segregated waste was wet, 20 percent was dry
recyclable, and 70 percent was inert.
All unsegregated waste was sent to a sorting plant. From unsegregated waste, 10 percent was
recovered as wet compostable waste, 30 percent was recovered as dry recyclable waste, and the
remaining 60 percent was sent to landfill. Wet waste sent to the compost facility produced
compost equal to 40 percent of wet input, while the remaining 60 percent became residue sent
to landfill. Dry recyclable waste sent to the recycling facility produced saleable recyclables
equal to 85 percent of dry input, while the remaining 15 percent became residue sent to
landfill.
Compost was sold at Rs. 2,500 per tonne, saleable recyclables were sold at Rs. 6,000 per tonne,
and landfill handling cost was Rs. 900 per tonne.
passages.QUA-P0115:
XIX. He doesn’t quite crash land but takes form all of a sudden – a life-size apparition in
uniform, if you find yourself in Seoul’s popular Jeo Dong Park. Don’t let him spook you – it’s
only a hologram of a cop, appearing every two minutes between 7pm and 10pm to, well, spook
those up to no good. Police claim the made-in-UK ‘assistant officer’ lowered crime rates in the
bustling neighbourhood under Seoul Jungbu police station by as much as 22%, between Oct
2024, when the pilot was launched, and May 2025. The cop was officially posted in the park
in Aug. So, if you’re wandering around, under the influence of whatever’s your poison, and
itching to pick up a fight, well, chances are the sight of a ghostly cop could nudge you to
abandon the idea. No need to break into a cold sweat or run, for he’ll disappear in two minutes.

So what does this hologram cop do if it comes across a fight? He can’t chase, let alone handcuff
you. Yet. ‘Enhanced features’ are work in progress. His role now is surveillance, a deterrent to
low-key ‘impulsive’ crime. Privacy may be globally dead but still, the idea hasn’t gone down
well with everyone. Visitors find him annoying, while his ghostly presence is fast creating an
urban legend of a ‘haunted park’. Clearly, tech savvy policing is not yet a smooth walk in the
park.

SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/phantom-police/
passages.QUA-P0116:
XXI. During the winter tourist season in Manali, three friends- Aarav, Meher, and Zubin- started a
temporary travel-essentials kiosk near a busy viewpoint. The stall sold woollen caps, gloves,
thermos bottles, and rain covers. Since the business was only for the season, they decided to
run it in partnership and keep proper records of their capital, time of investment, and profit-
sharing arrangement.
At the beginning of the season, Aarav invested 780,000 in the business. Meher joined the
business 2 months later with a capital of %1,00,000. Zubin also invested at the start, putting in
%1,20,000, but after 5 months he withdrew %30,000 from his capital and continued with the
reduced amount for the rest of the season. The business ran for a total of 12 months.
The partners agreed that before dividing the final profit, 10% of the total annual profit would
first be kept aside for stall rent, transport charges, and storage expenses. After this deduction,
36,000 would be given to Meher as a fixed management allowance because she handled
supplier calls, tourist group orders, and daily stock updates. The remaining profit would then
be divided among Aarav, Meher, and Zubin in the ratio of their effective capitals multiplied by
the time for which those capitals remained invested.www.lawpreptutorial.com
At the end of the season, the kiosk earned a total profit of %4,80,000. The partners then sat
together to calculate how much each one should receive and how the shares would change if
one partner had invested for a different period or changed capital midway.

passages.QUA-P0119: A logistics company operates delivery vans between four nearby cities Arvind Nagar, Bhola Town, Chitra City, and Devgarh. Every morning, vans leave from the central warehouse carrying parcels. The usual speed of the van traveling to Arvind Nagar was constant on most days. However, on Monday, due to heavy traffic, the actual speed of the van became 20% lower than its usual speed. XXIV. The defining moral failure of the older generation toward contemporary youth is not, as
conventional wisdom might suggest, one of excessive severity or unreasonable expectation — it is,
far more insidiously, one of catastrophic under-demand, a condescending benevolence that
simultaneously overestimates our character and remains perpetually bewildered by our failure to
meet even its negligible standards. Consider the now-notorious photograph of a UCLA graduate
triumphantly brandishing a ChatGPT interface at his commencement ceremony — an image that
has inspired an exhausting proliferation of superficial commentary content to engage with it at its
most anodyne interpretation: that the student employed artificial intelligence to circumvent
academic assessments and thereby fraudulently obtain his degree. Academic dishonesty is neither
novel nor particularly illuminating as a cultural phenomenon; what is genuinely alarming — and
what virtually every commentator above a certain age demonstrably fails to comprehend — is the
totalising, systemic pervasiveness of AI integration across every stratum of contemporary
university life, a penetration so thorough that characterising it merely as sophisticated cheating
represents a categorical confusion masquerading as moral discernment. The metastatic
proliferation of artificial intelligence across elite American campuses constitutes nothing less than
a civilisational pathology, one threatening to transmute an entire cohort of intellectually capable
young people into a generation of cognitively atrophied dependents, whilst simultaneously
desecrating the university as an institution — whether conceived as a humanist sanctuary, an
ethical formation ground, or a utilitarian credentialing apparatus. The author's own trajectory of
disillusionment at the University of Chicago charts this oncological progression with clinical
precision: what initially manifested as a localised and largely contained phenomenon — fraternity
members receiving mediocre scores on Al-assisted assessments, a logic professor dismissing

ChatGPT's transparently fallacious reasoning -— underwent a _ discernible malignant
transformation, evidenced most starkly by a forty-percentage-point differential between take-home
and in-person examination performance observed during a subsequent teaching assistantship. The
primary site of this cancerous metastasis proved, with grim predictability, to be the business
economics specialisation — a recently instituted and broadly derided academic appendage, widely
regarded by serious students as an intellectually undemanding concession to credentialist
pragmatism — wherein the pedagogical architecture itself seems almost deliberately engineered to
accommodate, if not incentivise, cognitive outsourcing: perfunctorily graded problem sets, recycled
sample examinations, arithmetic of conspicuous simplicity, and lecture-slide reiteration
substituting for genuine intellectual engagement. In such an environment, where conscientious
attendance and authentic intellectual labour are rendered entirely superfluous to the attainment of
acceptable marks, the conditions for wholesale artificial intelligence dependency are not merely
permissive but structurally determinative — a truth whose gravity the generation responsible for
designing these institutions appears constitutionally unable to confront.

XXIII. The controversy erupted through channels that have become depressingly familiar: perceptive
readers identified conspicuously algorithmic prose within a published literary work, unleashed
their derision across social media platforms, and deployed Al-detection software that returned
damning verdicts — precipitating institutional paralysis among the organisations responsible for
the work's publication. At the epicentre stood Jamir Nazir, a virtually obscure Trinidadian writer
whose short story "The Serpent in the Grove" had secured regional recognition within the
prestigious Commonwealth Short Story Prize, earning both a £2,500 honorarium and publication in
Granta, the esteemed British literary journal — before online scrutineers gleefully dissected its
suspiciously mechanical cadences, its formulaic syntactic constructions, and its grotesquely
overwrought metaphors. Suspicion rapidly metastasised to encompass two additional prizewinners:
Malta's John Edward DeMicoli and India's Sharon Aruparayil, both of whose stories were flagged
by Al-detection platforms as substantially or entirely machine-generated. Aruparayil, uniquely
among the accused, issued a categorical denial, insisting that no artificial intelligence had

participated in any dimension of her creative process, though she conspicuously declined to furnish
the time-stamped manuscript drafts she claimed as exculpatory evidence — whilst separately
disavowing an Al-promoting blog post attributed to her by an Emirati research foundation. What
distinguishes this particular scandal from its predecessors is not the institutional embarrassment
of unwittingly platforming Al-generated literature — a phenomenon that has infiltrated outlets as
venerable as The New York Times and publishing houses of considerable distinction — but rather
the authors' unprecedented and collective refusal to acknowledge any algorithmic involveme nt
whatsoever. The Commonwealth Foundation's director general, Razmi Farook, opted for
circumspection over rigour, accepting the prizewinners' reassurances while explicitly
acknowledging that her organisation's legal constraints precluded challenging an author's stated
honesty purely on the basis of detector outputs. Granta's response proved equally equivocal — and
considerably more farcical — when its publisher elected to consult the AI chatbot Claude for an
adjudication on suspected AI authorship, a methodological absurdity that predictably intensified
rather than ameliorated public ridicule. The deeper systemic vulnerability exposed by this episode
is not merely technological but institutional: given that Al-detection platforms remain
demonstrably fallible — exhibiting documented false-positive biases against non-native English
writers — and given that rescinding literary prizes without incontrovertible evidence carries
formidable moral and legal implications, determined authors may have identified a pote nt
enforcement loophole. Meanwhile, scholars Emily Bender and Alex Hanna advocate something
rather more immediate: sustained, unapologetic public ridicule of derivative, algorithmically
hollowed prose as both cultural resistance and prophylactic standard-maintenance — a strategy
that, however informal, may ultimately prove more efficacious than any institutional review panel
in preserving the irreducibly human essence of authentic literary creation.

XIX. Directions for Questions 103-108: Relationship Note for this puzzle
Use the following standard meanings:
First cousins share the same grandparents.
Second cousins share the same great-grandparents but NOT the same grandparents.
First cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a first-cousin relationship.
Second cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a second-cousin relationship.
At the annual Malhotra Family Reunion, eight relatives sat around a circular table, all facing the
centre.
The eight people were Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, Isha, Manav, Tara, and Ved.
The family background was as follows:
* Govind and Leela were the common ancestors of the branch gathered here.
+ Their two sons were Prakash and Suresh.
+ Prakash had three children: one daughter, Asha; one son, Bimal; and one daughter, Chitra.
+ Asha had two children: one son, Neeraj, and one daughter, Kavya.

+ Bimal had one son, Rohan.
+ Chitra had two daughters, Simran and Isha.
- Suresh had one daughter, Nandini.
* Nandini had two children: one son, Manav, and one daughter, Tara.
* Manav had one son, Ved.
Thus, Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha belong to the same first-cousin generation. Except
for sibling pairs, they are first cousins of one another.
Manav and Tara are second cousins of Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha.
Ved is second cousin once removed to Neeraj, Kavya, Rohan, Simran, and Isha.
The seating clues are as follows:
+ Rohan sat immediately counterclockwise of Ved.
+ Simran sat immediately clockwise of Ved.
+ Kavya sat immediately clockwise of Simran.
* Rohan sat opposite Manav.
- Isha sat immediately clockwise of Manav.
+ Neeraj sat immediately clockwise of Isha.
* Tara sat immediately clockwise of Neeraj.
+ The sibling pair from Nandini's branch (Manav and Tara) were not seated adjacent to each
other.
After the reunion, the organiser claimed that the seating arrangement had worked well because no
one was seated only with members of their own family branch. Instead, relatives sat next to people
from different branches, encouraging a wider interaction and conversations across the entire family
rather than within small family groups.
A family historian disagreed. She argued that a successful dinner does not prove that the seating
pattern itself caused wider interaction. In her view, the conversation may have depended on
personal interests, age, profession, humour, or people speaking across the table rather than only to
those seated beside them.
The family committee decided to review the seating notes and feedback cards before deciding
whether to repeat the same seating principle next year.
passages.QUA-P0137:
XX. India’s mergers and acquisitions market is getting bigger, but quieter. Deal values hit
$14 billion in Q3 2025, up 50 per cent from the year before. Yet, fewer deals are closing.
Companies are doing larger but fewer transactions, and smaller deals are falling away.

Mergers are important because they offer real exits to shareholders, and enable firms to
grow bigger, allowing them to optimize economies of scale and create surplus for
consumers. For a government that wants to focus on ease of doing business and has
aspirations of a $7.3 trillion economy, months lost in tribunal queues carry a real cost to
shareholders and Indian firms wanting to grow.

In her Union Budget 2025 speech, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman offered a
diagnosis. Requirements and procedures for speedy approval of company mergers were to
be rationalised, and the scope for fast-track mergers widened. In September, the Ministry


of Corporate Affairs followed through. The Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and
Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2025 expanded the fast-track merger framework,
allowing unlisted companies with borrowings under Rs 200 crore, holding-subsidiary
mergers, and fellow subsidiary restructurings to bypass the tribunal entirely, getting
approval directly from the Regional Director.

It was an acknowledgement that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the single
window meant to speed up corporate restructuring, has become a bottleneck. At The
Professeer, we analysed 3,376 merger cases filed after 2021 across all benches to
understand exactly where deals go to wait. These cases account for a fifth of the caseload
of the tribunal today.

On paper, a merger through NCLT should take 90-120 days. First, the company files an
application. Let’s call it the First Motion, the green light to talk to stakeholders. The
tribunal decides whether shareholders and creditors need to formally vote, or if that
requirement can be waived. Then comes a 30-day window for regulators – the Regional
Director, Income Tax, Registrar of Companies, and others – to raise objections. Finally, the
company files a Second Motion, and the NCLT approves or rejects the scheme. This
approval may be conditional or unconditional.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “NCLT bottleneck hinders India’s M&A boom.
Govt’s fast-track framework ignores the real problem”, ThePrint.]

questions.directionsText: For the Multiple Choice Questions, select the correct alternative from the given choices. For the Non-Multiple Choice Questions, write your answer in the box provided.
questions.solution: Direct proportion means x = k(y² + 4) for some constant k. Substituting x = 39 when y = 3 gives 39 = k(9 + 4) = 13k, so k = 3. questions.questionText: The mean proportional between two numbers is 9. The third proportional of the same numbers is 6561. Find the greater of the 2 numbers.
questions.directionsText: For the Multiple Choice Questions, select the correct alternative from the given choices. For the Non-Multiple Choice Questions, write your answer in the box provided.
questions.solution: If the mean proportional of a and b is 9, then ab = 9² = 81. If the third proportional is 6561, then a : b = b : 6561, so b² = 6561a. Substituting a = 81/b gives b³ = 6561 × 81 = 531441, so b = 81 and a = 1. The greater number is 81.

questions.questionText: A writer gets a fixed amount for his book apart from of the royalty he gets per book sold. He gets ₹46000 and ₹66000 for 2000 and 3000 books sold respectively. Find his income per book when 6000 books are sold (in ₹).
questions.directionsText: For the Multiple Choice Questions, select the correct alternative from the given choices. For the Non-Multiple Choice Questions, write your answer in the box provided.
questions.solution: Let the fixed amount be F and the royalty per book be r. Then F + 2000r = 46000 and F + 3000r = 66000. Subtracting gives 1000r = 20000, so r = 20 and F = 6000. For 6000 books the total is 6000 + 6000 × 20 = 126000, and income per book is 126000 ÷ 6000 = 21. Note the answer is not 20: the fixed amount is spread across the books too.

employees working in department P is 40 years. If the average age of males and average age of
females of department P are same as that of department R, respectively, then find the average
age of all the employees working in department R?
questions.solution: Average age of females working in department P = average age of total employees - average age of male employees = [40800 - 480x42]/320 = 37 So, required average age of all the employees working in department R = [450 x 42 + 750 x 37]/1200 = 46650/1200 = 38.875 years

questions.questionText:
Compare the Quantities and show the relationship between the two.
Quantity 1: New Manufacturer D has two vessels of equal volume containing the mixture of Isopropyl
Alcohol and gel base in the ratio of 4:3 and 3:2 respectively. If the mixture of two Vessels is mixed to
form a new mixture, then the quantity of gel base in the third Vessel is 58 liters. Find the quantity of
Isopropyl! Alcohol in the third Vessel?
Quantity 2: If manufacturer B changes his manufacturing technique, i.e. ratio of Isopropyl Alcohol and
Gel base in vessel P is 5 : 3 and same mixture in vessel Q in the ratio of 3 : 2, 16 liters of mixture from
vessel P is taken out and poured into vessel Q and the new ratio of Isopropyl Alcohol to gel base in Q
becomes 29 : 19. If new quantity of mixture in vessel Q is equal to initial quantity of mixture in vessel
P, then find quantity of Isopropy! Alcohol after 16 liters of mixture has been taken out from vessel P ?
questions.solution: Quantity 1 Ratio of Isopropyl Alcohol and gel base in the third Vessel = [(4/7) + (3/5)]: [(8/7) + (2/5)] =41:29 Thus, quantity of Isopropyl Alcohol in third vessel = (41/29)*58=82 liters Quantity 2 Let ratio of Isopropyl Alcohol and gel base in vessel P be 5x and 3x And ratio of Isopropyl Alcohol and gel base in vessel Q be 3y and 2y Given: (3y + 16 * 5/8)/ (2y + 16 * 3/8) = 29/19 (3y + 10)/ (2y+ 6) = 29/19 58y — 57y = 190 —- 174 y=16 New quantity of mixture in vessel Q = (16 x 3+10)+(16 x 2+6)
